topPRs.title: feat(proxyd): new proxyd_http_request_by_method_duration_seconds metric
topPRs.author: yashvardhan-kukreja
topPRs.body:
Signed-off-by: Yashvardhan Kukreja <yashvardhan@oplabs.co>

## Summary

Adds `proxyd_http_request_by_method_duration_seconds`, a per-method summary of HTTP JSON-RPC latency. The existing `proxyd_http_request_duration_seconds` series is unchanged. It still times every HTTP request, including GET /healthz and WebSocket connections, with no method_name label.

`method_name` is bounded by `rpc_method_mappings`. Batches are labeled `<batch>`, requests rejected before a method is known are labeled `unknown`, and `proxyd_healthz` keeps its own name. WebSocket connections and `GET /healthz` are excluded.

## Test plan

- [ ] `go test ./ -run 'TestHTTPRequestByMethodDuration|TestHTTPRequestMethodLabel'`
- [ ] Confirm the new series appears on `/metrics` for a single call, a batch, and a rejected request, and that an unlisted method increments `method_not_allowed` rather than creating a new series.

### HTTP/2 server memory exhaustion due to Trailer headers in net/http
[CVE-2026-78659](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-78659) / [GO-2026-6603](https://pkg.go.dev/vuln/GO-2026-6603)

<details>
<summary>More information</summary>

#### Details
When "Trailer" headers are sent by a client, the HTTP server internally uses the header values to populate the Request.Trailer map passed to the server handler. Because Request.Trailer is a map, each entry incurs memory overhead. For HTTP/2 servers, a malicious client can exploit this by sending a "Trailer" header that declares a large number of fields, causing the server to allocate a disproportionate amount of memory while bypassing Server.MaxHeaderValueCount and Server.MaxHeaderBytes limits. This exploit is not applicable for HTTP/1 servers, which do not support multiplexing a large number of requests over one TCP connection, and whose Server.MaxHeaderBytes are calculated differently.

#### Severity
Unknown

#### References
- [https://go.dev/cl/847185](https://go.dev/cl/847185)
- [https://go.dev/cl/847314](https://go.dev/cl/847314)
- [https://go.dev/issue/81857](https://go.dev/issue/81857)
- [https://groups.google.com/g/golang-announce/c/U2fTuyDJznI](https://groups.google.com/g/golang-announce/c/U2fTuyDJznI)

</details>

### HTTP/2 transport accepts malformed framing-related headers in net/http
[CVE-2026-78660](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-78660) / [GO-2026-6610](https://pkg.go.dev/vuln/GO-2026-6610)

<details>
<summary>More information</summary>

#### Details
Historically, we have been rather lax about malformed framing-related headers in our HTTP/2 implementation, as they cannot interfere with HTTP/2 framing. However, this makes it possible for our HTTP/2 implementation to forward responses containing such headers to an HTTP/1 client when acting as a reverse proxy. If the HTTP/1 client also does not behave strictly enough, this can result in response smuggling.

#### Severity
Unknown

### Excessive CPU consumption from repeated initial window changes in net/http
[CVE-2026-78669](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-78669) / [GO-2026-6611](https://pkg.go.dev/vuln/GO-2026-6611)

<details>
<summary>More information</summary>

#### Details
A malicious HTTP/2 peer can cause excessive CPU consumption in the client or server by opening a large number of streams and then sending many small SETTINGS frames containing SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE values.

### Double flow control refund on HTTP/2 server streams in net/http
[CVE-2026-78663](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-78663) / [GO-2026-6612](https://pkg.go.dev/vuln/GO-2026-6612)

<details>
<summary>More information</summary>

#### Details
The HTTP/2 server can refund connection-level flow control twice for the same data: Once when a client resets a stream (refunding data for any sent-but-unread portion of the stream), and again when a request handler reads the buffered data. A malicious client can exploit this to bypass the configured connection-level flow control limit (MaxReceiveBufferPerConnection). Total buffered data is still limited by the concurrent stream limit and stream-level flow control.

#### Severity
Unknown

### HTTP/2 server crash due to HPACK encoder race in net/http
[CVE-2026-97032](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-97032) / [GO-2026-6617](https://pkg.go.dev/vuln/GO-2026-6617)

<details>
<summary>More information</summary>

#### Details
HTTP/2 servers could end up crashing due to inadvertently modifying its HPACK encoder concurrently. This happens because the server modifies the HPACK encoder from two goroutines without synchronization: one uses the encoder to encode a HEADERS frame as part of a response sent to a client and the other modifies the encoder's table size when handling a SETTINGS frame containing SETTINGS_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE that a client sends. A malicious client can repeatedly send a request while changing the header table size to crash the server.

#### Severity
Unknown

topPRs.title: feat(proxyd): tx_validation_middleware: configurable max connections per host and max idle connections
topPRs.author: yashvardhan-kukreja
topPRs.body:
Signed-off-by: Yashvardhan Kukreja <yashvardhan@oplabs.co>

<!-- Contributions welcome! See https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/.github/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md -->

### Problem
The tx validation middleware's HTTP client hardcodes `MaxConnsPerHost=10`. DUe to this, during traffic bursts, a few slow validation calls can fill every connection, and later requests queue behind them.

The validation timeout starts before the request is sent, so time spent waiting for a connection counts against it. Under load, queued requests reach the validation service with little time left. They either time out, failing open or closed depending on `fail_open`, or add seconds of latency to tx submission, even when the validation service itself responds quickly.

`MaxIdleConnsPerHost` was also unset, so Go's default of 2 applied. After each burst, all but 2 connections were closed and had to be re-dialed on the next one.

### Changes
- Add `max_conns_per_host` and `max_idle_conns` to `[tx_validation_middleware]`. Both default to **30**, up from 10, and unset or non-positive values fall back to the default.
- Set `MaxIdleConnsPerHost` to `max_idle_conns`. The client only talks to a single host, so the two limits are equivalent.
- Document the new options in `example.config.toml`.

### Upgrade notes
- **No config changes are required.** Existing deployments get the higher defaults automatically.
- **Validation service load:** the service may now receive up to 30 concurrent requests per proxyd instance. Operators whose service can't handle that can lower `max_conns_per_host`.
- **Timeout behavior is unchanged:** time spent waiting for a connection still counts against `timeout_seconds`.

topPRs.title: replica-healthcheck: run compiled output with production dependencies
topPRs.author: falcorocks
topPRs.body:
## Summary

The replica-healthcheck runtime image copied the full builder tree, including devDependencies, and started the service through npm and ts-node. The two High advisories in the published image (braces 3.0.3, which has no fixed release, and nanoid 3.3.17) are only reachable through devDependency tooling that the service never loads at runtime.

The runtime stage now installs production dependencies only, runs the compiled dist/src/service.js with node, and no longer installs npm. The service still reads its configuration from environment variables. ts-node remains available for local development through yarn start. No dependency versions changed.
